name: Vibravox
description: Vibravox is a GDPR-compliant dataset containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone, plus an airborne microphone as reference. The corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are included. The dataset contains four subsets: speech-clean, speech-noisy, speechless-clean, and speechless-noisy, in French.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
publisher: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through a controlled recording protocol where 200 participants wore six simultaneous audio sensors (five body-conduction sensors and one airborne reference microphone) and performed four sequential tasks: reading sentences in quiet conditions (speech-clean), remaining silent in a noisy environment (speechless-noisy), remaining silent in complete silence (speechless-clean), and speaking in a noisy environment (speech-noisy). Noise was delivered via a 56-loudspeaker spherical array 3D spatializer. The Zoom F8n field recorder captured all six sensor signals simultaneously at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution.
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained after post-processing, with 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded. Issues included mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, microphones inadvertently left unequipped, and cases where a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from six simultaneous sensors per participant: headset microphone (Shure WH20XLR), forehead accelerometer (Knowles BU23173-000), in-ear soft foam microphone (Knowles FG-23329-P07), in-ear rigid earpiece microphone (Knowles SPH1642HT5H), throat microphone (iXradio XVTM822D-D35), and temple vibration pickup (AKG C411). Text for participant readings originated from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set and in-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel to attenuate low-frequency noise and artifacts. Voice Activity Detection (VAD) timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% in training, 10% in development/validation, and 10% in test sets, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Three automatic filters were applied to the speech-clean subset: (1) Phoneme Error Rate filter discarding samples where PER > 10%, computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; (2) SNR filter requiring SNR[i,j] = L_speech_50[i,j] - L_silence_50[i,j] > 1.5 dB to verify sensor functioning; (3) Sensitivity drift filter requiring L_speech_50[i,j] > L_silence_50[i] to detect sensitivity drift. All three other subsets (speech-noisy, speechless-clean, speechless-noisy) were included if the corresponding participant's speech-clean subset was not empty. Text was filtered to exclude proper names (except common first names, French town/region/country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Text normalization included lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with 33 French phonemes using the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For words where the phonemizer produced language switches, manual phonetic transcription was performed. Text transcriptions were sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice and filtered/normalized. The whisper-timestamped model was used for Voice Activity Detection to identify speech and silence segments.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: CoML lab text phonemizer (https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.03958); whisper-timestamped model (https://github.com/linto-ai/whisper-timestamped)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled phonetic transcription and phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded. The suprasegmental phenomenon of 'liaison' in French caused all models to either omit or add [z] as top errors, which was noted and excluded from phonetic confusion analysis.
rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male). Female participants: mean age 25.9 years, median age 22 years, min age 19 years, max age 59 years. Male participants: mean age 31.4 years, median age 27 years, min age 18 years, max age 82 years. Overall: mean age 28.55 years, median age 25 years, min age 18 years, max age 82 years. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model for Voice Activity Detection and word timestamp prediction; CoML lab text phonemizer for IPA phonetic transcription; Whisper for speech-to-text used in PER computation during post-processing filtering
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available on HuggingFace under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The dataset is versioned (revision 071945b referenced in the paper). Code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jhauret/vibravox.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are collected and reported in dataset statistics. Voice recordings inherently contain biometric information. The dataset includes speaker identity information enabling speaker verification. The paper notes that body-conducted signals may be more descriptive of a person's identity due to unique skull and timbre characteristics. All data collection was conducted in compliance with GDPR, with informed consent obtained, data anonymized and encrypted during storage and analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, and intelligence gathering. The dataset could enable voice commands for heavy machinery operation and monitoring of vital signs including heart rate. The authors note potential military applications including access control and speaker identification in intercepted transmissions.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is in French only, restricting applicability to French language research. The Lombard effect (speakers increasing vocal effort in noisy conditions) means reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on actual values. Some participants had ear canals too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, which was not always caught by the automatic filters. The dataset may not fully represent all acoustic scenarios encountered in real-world applications.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is exclusively in French. The speech-noisy subset lacks a clean reference, limiting its use primarily to testing rather than training. The in-ear microphone design follows a 'one-size-fits-all' approach, which may not provide adequate acoustic sealing for all ear canal anatomies. Body-conduction sensors exhibit reduced bandwidth compared to airborne microphones, with the temple sensor barely recording speech above 1500 Hz and the laryngophone showing coherence dropping below 0.25 at 2000 Hz. The dataset cannot be used to produce realistic synthetic data due to the inadequacy of assuming a simple transfer function between airborne and body-transmitted speech.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Validation, and Testing for: speech enhancement/bandwidth extension, automatic speech recognition (speech-to-phonemes), speaker verification, and physiological sound analysis (heart rate tracking). The speech-clean subset is the primary training resource. The speech-noisy subset serves primarily for testing. The speechless-clean subset is useful for analyzing noise properties of sensors and generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological noise. The speechless-noisy subset can be dynamically mixed with speech-clean for data augmentation to simulate noisy conditions while retaining a clean reference.
